subject: red acidic river
title: What If a River Ran Blood Red for 5,000 Years? Spain's Does

scenes.text: What if a river ran blood red for 5,000 years? In Spain, one does, and NASA studies it.
The Rio Tinto flows about 100 kilometres from the hills of southern Spain to the Atlantic, red the whole way.
Its water sits around pH 2, about as acidic as vinegar. Drop in a fish and it dies.
The colour is dissolved iron. The hills are packed with pyrite, fool's gold, mined for copper and silver for about 5,000 years.
Yet the river is alive. Acid-loving microbes thrive in it, some living on iron and sulphur alone, and algae coat the red rocks.
That is why NASA came. Rusty, acidic and iron-rich: it is the closest thing on Earth to a river on ancient Mars.

description:
What if a river ran blood red for thousands of years? Spain's Rio Tinto does.
The river flows about 100 km through the Huelva mining district to the Atlantic with water around pH 2, as acidic as vinegar, coloured deep red by dissolved iron leached from pyrite-rich rock. The area has been mined for roughly 5,000 years. Despite the acid, the river is full of acid-loving microbes and algae, which is why NASA's astrobiology programme has used it as a stand-in for ancient Mars, even drilling its riverbed to rehearse a Mars drilling mission.
